transcript.text: Welcome back to Small Rooms, a podcast about people who build things in small spaces.
This episode is completely fictional and made up for a software demo.
My guest today is Rana Vell, who runs a pottery studio called Lantern Clay.
Rana, thanks for coming on the show.
Thank you for having me, I'm really happy to be here.
So let's start at the very beginning.
How did you end up making pottery for a living?
Honestly, it started by accident.
I was working in an office job that I didn't love, and a friend dragged me to a pottery class one evening.
I remember the first time I put my hands on the wet clay on the wheel.
It collapsed into a mess, and everyone laughed, including me.
But something about the wheel felt calm in a way my office never did.
After that I went back every single week.
Within a year I had bought a second hand wheel and a tiny electric kiln and set them up in my garage.
The garage was so small that I had to move my car out every time I fired the kiln.
My neighbours thought I was running some kind of strange factory.
Um, you know, I sold my first bowls at a weekend market, like, for almost nothing.
And, uh, I basically gave half of them away to friends.
So when did it stop being a hobby?
That's when the flood happened.
Three years ago a storm flooded the whole street, and the water came straight into the garage.
I lost everything in one night: the wheel, the kiln, the glazes, two hundred finished pieces.
I was terrified, and I sat on the steps and cried for an hour.
I thought it was over, and I honestly thought about going back to the office for good.
Then something happened that I never expected.
The next morning my students and neighbours showed up with buckets and mops.
A woman I had never met set up an online fundraiser, and in one week strangers raised enough to buy a new kiln.
That was the moment I realised this was not a hobby anymore.
People cared about the studio, and I owed it to them to take it seriously.
The lesson I took from the flood is simple: you are never as alone as you feel on the worst night.
Wow, that is a powerful story.
What did you do with that new kiln?
I rented a small unit behind a bakery and turned it into a real studio.
It's warm in there all year because of the bakery ovens next door.
I started teaching evening classes for beginners, four students at a time.
Teaching changed everything for the business.
The classes paid the rent, and the students became my most loyal customers.
Some of them still come every Thursday, five years later.
And how did you build a team?
Slowly, and with a lot of mistakes.
My first hire was an apprentice who had more talent than me but no patience.
We argued about glazes every day, and after six months he left.
I was angry for a while, but he taught me that I needed clear rules, not just good vibes.
Now every apprentice gets a written plan for their first ninety days.
They know what they will learn, what they will make, and how they will be paid.
Here's the thing nobody tells you about hiring: people don't leave because the work is hard, they leave because they don't know where they stand.
That's such a useful point.
Let's talk about money, because a lot of makers struggle with pricing.
How do you decide what a mug costs?
For years I priced everything by guessing what people would pay.
That was my biggest mistake.
I was selling mugs for less than the clay, the glaze and the electricity cost me.
One winter my electricity bill was higher than my sales, and I finally sat down with a spreadsheet.
I worked out the real cost of every piece, including my own time at a fair hourly rate.
Then I doubled most of my prices overnight.
I was so nervous, I was sure the customers would disappear.
They didn't.
A few people complained, but most of them said they had always thought the mugs were too cheap.
My advice to any maker is this: if you don't know your real cost, you are not running a business, you are running a very expensive hobby.
What about wholesale, selling to shops?
Wholesale is tricky, because shops usually want half the retail price.
I only sell wholesale for simple pieces that I can make quickly in batches.
The special pieces, the big platters and vases, I keep for the studio shop and the markets.
Cash flow is the other thing.
Shops often pay sixty days after delivery, so you need savings or you will be in trouble.
Um, so, yeah, that's kind of, like, the money side, I guess.
Let's move to the last part of the conversation.
If someone listening wants to turn their craft into a business, where should they start?
Start small and start before you feel ready.
You don't need a big studio, you need ten people who love what you make.
Talk to those ten people, ask what they would pay, and listen carefully.
And keep a little money aside, because one bad night can change everything.
I learned that the hard way with the flood.
What are you most proud of?
I'm most proud that the studio feels like a home for people.
A retired teacher told me last month that our Thursday class is the best part of her week.
When I heard that, I honestly had tears in my eyes.
That means more to me than any sales number.
What's next for Lantern Clay?
We are planning a second small studio in another neighbourhood next year.
Same idea, small classes, warm room, good clay.
Rana, thank you so much for sharing your story.
Thank you, this was a lot of fun.
And thanks to everyone listening to Small Rooms.
Remember, this episode is fictional, and so is everyone in it.
